questions.prompt: How do you decide which tool or format to use for a learning project?
questions.answer: I am not very attached to a specific tool. I start with what the learner actually has to do, how much time they have, how often the content will change, and what the delivery environment can support. If a short Rise module solves it, I do not turn it into a giant Storyline build. If the learner needs to make decisions, I will use Storyline or a custom interaction. If the problem is reference-heavy, a job aid may be better than a course. I like having a broad toolset because it gives me more ways to solve the problem without forcing every request into the same format.

questions.prompt: How quickly can you learn a new authoring tool, LMS, or platform?
questions.answer: Pretty quickly. I care more about understanding the underlying job than memorizing one interface. Once I know the content model, publishing rules, data flow, and what the tool is good or bad at, I can usually transfer what I already know from other authoring systems, LMS platforms, design tools, or code. That is how I have moved between classroom technology, Articulate, Adobe tools, LMS administration, automation, and web-based prototyping. I would rather be known as someone who can learn the next tool than someone whose value disappears when a company changes software.

questions.prompt: How do you decide whether something should be training at all?
questions.answer: I try not to solve every problem with a course. If someone needs to remember a concept, practice a decision, or build confidence before doing something, training can make sense. If they mainly need a reference at the moment of work, I would rather give them a usable job aid, checklist, searchable resource, or short performance-support asset. I also look for system or process problems before calling something a learning problem. That usually keeps the learning smaller and more useful.

questions.prompt: What do you do when a stakeholder wants to put everything into the training?
questions.answer: That happens a lot with technical products. I usually bring the conversation back to the learner's job: what do they need to recognize, explain, decide, or do after this? Then I map the requested content against those decisions. Important reference material can still exist, but it does not all need equal weight inside the learning. I am comfortable saying, 'This is accurate and useful information, but it is not necessary for this audience in this moment.' That is one of the places where I think an instructional designer earns their keep.

questions.prompt: What do you do when you disagree with a subject matter expert or stakeholder?
questions.answer: I try to separate factual ownership from design ownership. If an SME tells me something is technically wrong, that is their lane and I need to fix it. If the disagreement is about putting six screens of detail in front of a seller who only needs one decision, that is where I will push back and explain the learning consequence. I usually make the tradeoff visible instead of turning it into a taste argument: audience, objective, time, cognitive load, maintenance cost, and what behavior we are actually trying to change.

questions.prompt: How do you work when the source material is incomplete, inconsistent, or changing?
questions.answer: I expect source material to be messy, especially around product launches. I build a source-of-truth trail first, flag contradictions instead of quietly resolving them myself, and separate stable learning architecture from details that are likely to change. I also try to make the course modular enough that one product update does not force a rebuild of everything around it. If a decision is still pending, I would rather leave a visible placeholder in development than publish a confident guess.

questions.prompt: How do you balance speed, polish, and accuracy when a project has a tight deadline?
questions.answer: I prioritize the parts that create risk first: accuracy, learner path, completion behavior, and the decisions the learner has to make. Visual polish matters to me, but I will not spend three hours perfecting animation while the assessment logic is still wrong. I like reusable patterns because they let me move faster without making every project look generic. On tight launch work, I also separate what must be ready for day one from what can be improved in the next maintenance pass.

questions.prompt: What does high-quality instructional design mean to you?
questions.answer: For me, good instructional design is not the fanciest course. It is learning that respects the audience, gets the content right, gives people a useful chance to think or practice, and works inside the system where it has to live. I also care a lot about whether someone else can maintain it six months later. A beautiful course that is confusing, impossible to update, or disconnected from the learner's job is still a bad deliverable.

questions.prompt: What can you own independently without a lot of hand-holding?
questions.answer: Give me the audience, business need, access to the right source material and people, and a clear approval path, and I can usually take the work a long way independently. I am comfortable scoping, organizing source content, designing the learning architecture, building in authoring tools, creating visuals and multimedia, coordinating review, testing in the LMS, documenting issues, and handling the operational pieces around launch. I ask questions early when something affects accuracy or ownership, but I do not need someone to prescribe every screen or interaction for me.

questions.prompt: How do you design learning that will be maintained after launch?
questions.answer: I try to design the maintenance model while I am designing the learning. That means keeping volatile product details from being duplicated across five places, documenting which source owns which claims, building reusable components where they actually help, and separating regional or optional material when it has a different update cycle. I have inherited enough changing product content to know that maintenance is not an afterthought. It is part of the design.

questions.prompt: What would you change if you could redo one of your strongest projects?
questions.answer: On the certification work, I would define some of the operational rules earlier, especially routing, reporting, source ownership, and certification logic. The learning itself can be well designed and still create extra work later if those surrounding rules are fuzzy. I would also push the final assessment further toward performance-based seller decisions instead of letting any unnecessary recall creep in. That project taught me to design the course and the operating model together much earlier.

questions.prompt: What would make you valuable on an instructional design team?
questions.answer: I can move between the learning problem and the stuff around it. I am comfortable doing the actual instructional design, building the course, making the visuals, editing media, working in the LMS, troubleshooting the learner path, looking at reporting, and using code when there is repetitive work worth automating. I also came from teaching, so I care about whether another human can actually understand and use what I build. I think my strongest value is that I do not stop at 'the course is published.' I tend to notice the surrounding workflow and fix what I reasonably can.
